frontmatter.description: The same bounded sampled optimizer on a triangle MaxCut task and a second stated two-qubit Hamiltonian.

children.value: couple three sampling seeds to different initial angles. Here we reuse the same circuit generators and sampled polling rule on two changed inputs, while holding each task’s initial angles fixed across seeds. This separates sampling-seed variation from initialization changes within these runs. It tests a small amount of implementation portability rather than large-instance performance of QAOA or VQE

The three seeds, initial angles, 32-sweep schedule, measurement groups, and post-training targets are declared before the runs. Results are reported for every seed, including target misses. The inputs and schedule are not retuned after seeing outcomes.

Counts are ideal samples drawn classically from explicit circuit probabilities. Exact reference values are post-training diagnostics. A successful toy run does not establish convergence, a hardware success probability, or an advantage over the independent classical solution.

This portability check applies the same bounded sampled optimizer to two new toy inputs: the three-vertex triangle MaxCut graph with all three edges, and the Hamiltonian H = -0.8 Z0 - 0.6 Z1 + 0.4 X0X1 with the same RY/CX ansatz. All eight classical cut assignments give optimum 2; full matrix diagonalization gives ground energy -sqrt(2.12). Changed problem inputs prevent a same-task resource comparison with earlier reports.

objectives. Ideal measurement outcomes are generated from statevector probabilities; exact expectations are used only for post-decision diagnostics. They are modeled ideal measurements, rather than executed hardware shots.

The bounded schedule contains four blocks of eight sweeps: (step radians, shots/group) = (0.4, 256), (0.2, 512), (0.1, 1024), (0.05, 2048). The initial objective uses 256 shots/group. Each sweep freshly measures its incumbent and both coordinate proposals for every parameter, including all rejected proposals. A candidate is accepted only when the sampled decrease exceeds twice the combined estimated standard error; this margin is a heuristic, without a confidence or convergence guarantee across adaptive choices. Every run stops after the prescribed 32 sweeps.

Seeds 7, 19 and 41 use the same fixed initialization for each task: QAOA (0.2, 0.1), VQE (0.6). Only the seeded measurement randomness changes within each task. Three observed runs do not certify a population success probability. No target-based retuning is performed. Fresh validation uses 4,096 shots per group and a separate keyed random-stream family after training ends.

Fresh validation estimates the energy or expected cut of the final, already selected state. The estimated standard error includes within-group covariance; it is not a rigorous interval. A zero empirical standard error can occur when a finite sample contains only one score and does not certify the exact mean. The separate Hoeffding radius is an ideal-sampling 95% bound for each validation row, not simultaneous table coverage.

The post-run numerical targets are exact expected cut at least 1.90 for QAOA and exact energy gap at most 0.03 for VQE. These diagnostics assess the selected toy states after training; target flags are not guarantees derived from the validation confidence bound. Separately, the fresh validation has an absolute expectation-error target of 0.10 at 95% confidence for one fixed estimate. The displayed Hoeffding radii determine whether that readout allocation supports this precision target.

QAOA seed 7: fresh validation observed best cut 2 (classical optimum 2); the sampled optimal-cut fraction was 0.999756. The fixed final state’s exact optimal-cut probability, audited after training, was 0.999526.

QAOA seed 19: fresh validation observed best cut 2 (classical optimum 2); the sampled optimal-cut fraction was 1.000000. The fixed final state’s exact optimal-cut probability, audited after training, was 0.999526.

QAOA seed 41: fresh validation observed best cut 2 (classical optimum 2); the sampled optimal-cut fraction was 0.999512. The fixed final state’s exact optimal-cut probability, audited after training, was 0.999526.

. The full CPU workflow took 0.709759 s. Simulator/probability generation and classical search work are software timings rather than quantum runtime. Logical counts repeat every preparation, measurement basis change, and readout for all training and validation shots. Arbitrary rotations remain unsynthesized. Physical reset/measurement timing, routing, faults, error correction, factories, hardware latency, noise and mitigation are excluded; physical resource estimates remain pending.

children.value: The schedule uses 161 QAOA training calls and 97 VQE training calls per seed. All proposals, incumbent remeasurements, the initial call, and fresh final holdout count. Across the three seeds, the circuit protocol represents 473,856 QAOA shots and 579,072 VQE shots, totaling 1,052,928. The
maps every measured group and its basis changes, gates, and qubit readout. These protocol totals are not measured hardware consumption; the implementation generates counts classically.

The original four-vertex cycle and first Hamiltonian remain separate baseline cases. A smaller triangle uses fewer qubits and edges, but it is a different problem with a different objective maximum and target. The two Hamiltonians also have different coefficients and energy scales. The original runs vary initialization, and the new cases use separate random streams; comparing equal seed labels across experiments mixes input, initialization, and random-stream changes. Equal optimizer schedules do not turn their logical counts or empirical target outcomes into matched-problem physical improvements. No claim of quantum advantage, transferable convergence, or a general success rate follows from these comparisons.
